Language across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

Vocabulary

Between ages 9 and 12, children’s vocabulary grows explosively, both in size and in depth of understanding. A 9-year-old’s lexicon, though large, is still rooted in everyday conversational words and concrete terms. By 12, children have acquired thousands of new words, including the academic and abstract vocabulary needed for school learning 1. This reflects the mid-childhood shift from "learning to read" to "reading to learn," which typically occurs by 4th grade (around age 9-10) 2. As 12-year-olds read textbooks and broader literature, they encounter and master specialized terms in science, math, and social studies (e.g. photosynthesis, fraction, government), words rarely found in casual conversation at age 9 1. Morphological sophistication continues to accelerate as derivational morphology becomes increasingly productive, allowing children to parse and generate novel forms with greater facility than at nine 3, 4, 1; they parse unfamiliar words into bases plus affixes, use Greek/Latin combining forms to triangulate meanings (photo-/bio-/-logy, electro-/-magnet-/-ism), and flexibly shift parts of speech via nominalizations and adjectival derivations that saturate textbooks (predict->prediction; molecule->molecular) 3. This shift goes beyond the robust 7-9 surge: knowledge of derived forms and multi-morphemic items becomes a principal driver of vocabulary expansion through late elementary and into middle school 5, and performance on derived-word tasks and CALS (Core Academic Language Skills) assessments increasingly predicts reading comprehension in informational text. Syntax

Children’s sentence structures also undergo a marked increase in complexity. By age 9, most children command the fundamental grammar of their language and produce complex sentences in conversation; however, their sentences tend to be relatively short (on the order of 7 words; e.g "I went to the pool and swam") and tied to familiar structures. By age 12, children can reliably comprehend and generate much more elaborate syntax 6, 1, including subordinate clauses, conditional sentences, and varied word orders 1 that were challenging at 9. There is a clear rise in the use of multi-clause sentences 7: for example, a 12-year-old might say or write, "I did my homework after I ate dinner because I wanted to watch TV later," comfortably embedding adverbial and causal clauses. In fact, one study notes that persuasive essays written by children this age heavily employ subordinate clauses and causal connectors as key linguistic resources 8, illustrating how syntax becomes a tool for organizing complex ideas. Comparatively, a 9-year-old’s persuasive attempt might rely on simpler coordination (e.g. stringing ideas with "and") rather than such embedded structures. Dual meanings

Semantic development between 9 and 12 years is characterized by a shift from concrete, literal interpretations toward a richer understanding of abstract and non-literal meaning. One important change is the handling of multiple-meaning words. A 9-year-old might recognize that some common words have more than one meaning (for example, "cold" as a temperature vs. "a cold" illness) and find simple jokes about homophones funny; however, by 12, children not only understand many polysemous words but can also explain the different meanings and how context determines the interpretation (e.g a 12-year-old can clarify that a "tie" you wear versus "to tie a knot" are related by a notion of joining but are used differently as noun and verb 1). They also become proficient in providing superordinate and subordinate relations among concepts (e.g. knowing that sparrow is a type of bird, which is a type of animal, etc.), and in understanding metaphorical categorizations (e.g. that "school can be a second home" is not literal but conveys an abstract relationship).

Figurative language

Perhaps the most noticeable leap in this age range is in figurative language comprehension and production. Children around age 9 are beginning to "get" some figurative expressions; they laugh at basic puns, enjoy simple similes or metaphors (like "as busy as a bee"), and may understand common idioms if given enough context. Yet, their interpretations can still be literal or incomplete. By age 12, many figurative forms that baffled younger children become intelligible (tracking with an overall "less literal understanding of language" 9). For example, 12-year-olds generally understand common idioms such as "knocked my socks off" or "in hot water", even if they might not articulate exactly why the phrases mean what they do 9, 1. Learning idioms and metaphors is certainly a gradual process, but by the end of childhood most kids can interpret at least the common idioms in context 1. They also start to grasp proverbs and more culturally bound figurative sayings by early adolescence; a 12-year-old may not fully explain a proverb like "A picture paints a thousand words" in the abstract, but can often interpret its meaning within a given context, a capability that typically solidifies in the years shortly after 12 1. Narratives and autobiography

Reflecting broader linguistic advancements, this window marks a significant transition in narrative and autobiographical memory, shifting from foundational storytelling (i.e acquisition of the abilities to include multiple episodes, evaluative comments, and causal chaining by age 9) to more organized, analytical, and integrated narrative comprehension and construction 10, 11, 12. Surfacing in both autobiographical and fictitious accounts, their narratives see substantial maturation both in terms of their coherence (i.e proposing a story structured in several steps at the temporal, causal and thematic levels; at the level of the overall macrostructure) 13, 14, 15 and cohesion (i.e the creation of links between two statements; at the microstructure level) 16, with some suggesting that these abilities begin to plateau (reaching near adult levels) around age 12 16, but other evidence suggesting that these abilities continue to grow more sophisticated/strategic well past this window (which aligns with naturalistic observations) 17, 18. Likewise, the specificity of remembered and imagined events increases, and children’s narratives become more semantically rich (i.e more consistently answering who-what-where-when-why and approaching greater "completeness") as shown longitudinally 19, 20. Despite these gains, 9-12-year-olds remain less likely than older adolescents and adults to fully integrate trait descriptors, second-order beliefs 21, and other social-cognitive information into their stories, with performance still sensitive to social-cognitive processing demands and the structural importance of that information 22. Overall, by age 12 there is a convergence between broad world knowledge (cause-effect relations, event schemas, protagonists’ goal-directed behavior) and knowledge of narrative conventions (e.g story grammar 23) to yield the ability to construct and revise multi-episode situation models that maintain global coherence while flexibly integrating local details during both comprehension and production. This window also foreshadows the adolescent turn toward identity/self-conceptual development, as youths increasingly leverage autobiographical memory and burgeoning narrative reasoning to assemble more coherent self-stories and explore commitments 24; by the midpoint of this window, children can understand periods in history, seem to have a fully developed ability to reason about time on an abstract level 25, and their tendency to group their life stories into coherent periods or "chapters" is increasing rapidly 26.
